subject: Pharmacology
summary: Unfractionated heparin (UFH) is an injectable anticoagulant that enhances antithrombin III, blocking thrombin and factor Xa. It is monitored by the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) to keep clotting within a therapeutic window.

sections.p: UFH is a heterogeneous mixture of glycosaminoglycans given intravenously or subcutaneously to prevent or treat thrombosis. Diagnosis of its effect relies on aPTT prolongation.
b: Short half‑life (~1 h) allows quick reversal

sections.p: Bleeding risk is graded by the intensity of aPTT elevation and clinical signs, not by a formal stage system.
Excess anticoagulation can result from dosing errors, renal/hepatic dysfunction, drug interactions, or underlying coagulopathies.
Patients may develop bruising, hematuria, gastrointestinal bleeding, or intracranial hemorrhage if anticoagulation is excessive.
Laboratory monitoring guides dosing and detects complications.

t.b: Is the anticoagulant effect within therapeutic range? Therapeutic 1.5–2.5× control; higher suggests bleeding risk.
Is HIT developing? A fall >50% or <150 ×10⁹/L after 5–10 days signals HIT.
Provides a direct measure of heparin activity when aPTT is unreliable (e.g., lupus anticoagulant). Target 0.3–0.7 IU/mL.

sections.p: Bleeding and heparin‑induced thrombocytopenia are the two life‑threatening complications.
Adjust UFH infusion based on aPTT, stop if bleeding, and treat HIT if present.
b: Reduce or pause infusion when aPTT >3× control
Switch to a direct thrombin inhibitor (e.g., argatroban) if HIT confirmed

sections.p: Regular aPTT checks (every 6 h after dose changes) and platelet monitoring (baseline, then every 2–3 days) prevent complications.
b: Educate patients on signs of bleeding
Avoid concurrent high‑dose aspirin/NSAIDs unless necessary

sections.p: Low‑molecular‑weight heparins (LMWH) and direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) have different monitoring and reversal strategies.
b: LMWH: monitored by anti‑Xa, longer half‑life
DOACs: no routine lab monitoring needed

sections.p: aPTT may be falsely normal in patients with lupus anticoagulant or high factor VIII levels, masking over‑anticoagulation.
b: Consider anti‑Xa testing if aPTT unreliable
Interpret platelet drop in context of heparin exposure

faq.q: Why is UFH monitored with aPTT and not PT/INR?
faq.a: UFH mainly prolongs the intrinsic pathway measured by aPTT; PT/INR reflects the extrinsic pathway and is not sensitive to UFH.

faq.q: Can UFH be used in patients with renal failure?
faq.a: Yes, because UFH is cleared by the reticuloendothelial system, not the kidneys.

faq.q: What is the antidote for UFH overdose?
faq.a: Protamine sulfate neutralizes UFH rapidly; dose is calculated from the amount of heparin given.

exam: Explain how UFH exerts its anticoagulant effect and why aPTT is used for monitoring.
Describe the clinical and laboratory features that suggest heparin‑induced thrombocytopenia.
Outline the steps to manage a patient with supratherapeutic aPTT and active bleeding.
